The saved catalog_2026-27.html holds only the home page (nav/title), so the 13 section pages (https://sites.google.com/ccsuvt.net/26-27programofstudies/<section>) were fetched with curl, converted to text and appended to phase2/text/twinfield-union-school.txt as '=== SECTION n (name) ===' blocks; source_page is the section number (2 Transitions, 3 Integrated Studies, 4 ELA, 5 Math, 6 Science, 7 World Language, 8 VPA, 9 Global Citizenship, 10 Health & PE, 11 Design Technology, 12 Renaissance, 13 More Student Opportunities, 14 VVLC); these pages were not saved under catalogs/. Status partial because the site gives no credits, and Visual & Performing Arts / Design Technology entries are brief; the Vermont Virtual Learning Coop page names no courses (links to an external catalog), so no VTVLC records. Courses cross-listed in two sections (Bioethics, Physics, Community Based Learning, Intro to Art & Design) are one record each. 'Not offered this year' Global Citizenship courses are included with offering_note; two older duplicate entries (Criminal Justice, US History honors text) are not recorded separately. Calculus I is dual enrollment (SNHU 3 credits). Graduation requirements come from the older grad_requirements_2022-23.pdf (v.9 4/23 guide; may be out of date); Twinfield uses proficiency-based graduation with no credit counts, so total_credits null and by_area empty. graduation_requirements.raw_text: To graduate, you must demonstrate proficiency or distinction in Twinfield’s twenty-eight content standards. The path to those content standards is through meeting indicators set up by each academic discipline.

courses.description: This class will discuss how to use what you have learned in high school that can be used towards your success in your next phase, whether it’s college, a gap year, or a new job. As the saying goes, happiness isn’t a destination, it’s a way to travel. So what do you have in your suitcase now? What will you need along the way? For college-bound students, we will look at a new set of study skills, how to take good notes, how to read a syllabus, visit with tutors and writing centers, talk to your professors, and most importantly, how to manage your time, so you can meet deadlines and still have time for yourself, sleep, and even reward yourself for a job well done. Other phases require many of the same skills, actually. So we will talk about the ways to identify what's working, or what you need help with, for example, how do you know if you are in the right major or job? What are some factors to consider?
courses.notes: Section heading: 'TRANSITIONS: Use what you know to shape your future'

courses.description: Bioethics will allow students to delve into a variety of controversial issues in society. Students will focus on issues through the lens of current scientific research, while also focusing on societal influences in the making of ethical decisions. In examining the morality of situations, students will formulate arguments based on scientific research, paying particular attention to supporting evidence. In addition, students will include in their arguments influences that are more difficult to quantify, such as background, personal experience, and religion. Students will also study literature, investigating how authors make connections to science and civilization and how science influences culture. Possible titles for study include The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks and Flowers for Algernon.

courses.course_name: Community Based Learning and Applied Science and ELA
courses.description: This class will explore everyday science by looking at situations that might arise in your home. We will look at the chemistry of cleaning products, scientific reactions in cooking, and how to approach different types of stains in the laundry. We will look at how to grow herbs in our kitchen and ways we can use food scraps to minimize waste. We will also try to explore student interests as they arise in conversation! Throughout our scientific explorations, students will also work on ELA indicators through reading informational texts, participating in discussions, and responding to writing prompts connected to our topics of study.

The literature studies will provide a base of knowledge for post-secondary study. Possible texts include The Once and Future King, Much Ado About Nothing, Flowers for Algernon, and Frankenstein. This class is for 12th graders or 11th graders who are planning on Early College.

courses.description: Math Lab provides student with the opportunity to either complete proficiencies and graduation requirements or receive regular support in mathematics. Students will be able to be supervised and supported while working at their own rate as they build their mathematical practice and understanding. The class will offer small group instruction and individual attention to the extent possible.
courses.notes: PBGR Math Indicators by class. Concepts addressed depend on individual needs.

courses.description: In this course students will study Algebra 1 to build understanding of Algebraic concepts and continue to develop problem solving and mathematical reasoning skills. Attention will be paid to ensuring students are comfortable and confident with the skills necessary for success using mathematics in class and life. By the end of the course, students will have the opportunity to complete all Algebra I indicators and proficiencies.
courses.notes: Indicators Addressed: Algebra 1 indicators

courses.description: In this course students will study Geometry and build their understanding of basic Geometric concepts as well as geometric logic, reasoning, proof and construction skills.

courses.description: Algebra 2 is recommended for students who are interested in post-secondary study. This course is a teacher-paced advanced Algebra class. The main focus is functions and equations beyond the scope of Algebra I including, but not limited to, quadratic, power, rational, polynomial, logarithmic and exponential. Students will learn to graph, solve, problem solve, and understand quadratic functions and solve quadratic equations. Students will also study polynomial, radical, and exponential functions.
courses.notes: Indicators addressed: Math (Beyond)

courses.description: Pre-Calculus is recommended for students who are interested in post-secondary study of mathematics, science as well as for admission at rigorous colleges. The focus of the course is a study of functions and modeling--algebraic, polynomial and rational, expnential, logarithmic and trigonometic. Trigonometry will include right triangle trig; basic trigonometric functions and their inverses; trig laws and applications; and proofs and identities. The course includes graphing technology to study problem situations analytically, graphically, and numerically.
courses.notes: Indicators Addressed: Math (Beyond)

courses.description: This course is a college course taught at Danville and available either in person or remotely. Topics include limits, differentiation, integration, logarithmic and exponential functions, and volume of solids of revolution. Students may choose to take the course for college credit through SNHU.

courses.description: Financial lit will introduce issues you will deal with every day. Some areas covered are earning and budgeting money, choosing a credit card, purchasing/owning an automobile, managing loans, the insurance game, taxes, investments and retirement, and other life challenges.

courses.description: This class will fulfill the Probabilty and Statistics graduation requirement. We will explore the fundamentals of probability, then dig into the power of statistical analysis. You will learn how to plan a study, collect and analyze data, and present your findings in a clear and honest way. You will also learn how to make sense of statistical findings presented in the media and in scientific literature. This class will prepare you to be a better citizen, and the skills and concepts you learn will be relevant for many career paths. Assessment will include tests, quizzes, and projects.
courses.fulfills_text: This class will fulfill the Probabilty and Statistics graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Taught by Caleb Corliss. Indicators Addressed: Math 4a, 4b, 4c, 4d

courses.description: This is a required course that will provide an introduction and overview to the physical sciences. Students will study large topics within the disciplines of Earth and Space Sciences. Part of the class will be taught as a standalone science course, and part will be taught as an integrated study with 9th grade English.
courses.notes: Part taught as standalone science, part integrated with 9th grade English. Indicators addressed: Science 6a-6e; Content indicators 2b, 3b, 5c

courses.course_name: 10th Grade Human Impact on the Biosphere/ELA Integrated
courses.description: This integrated full-year course combines Science and English Language Arts to explore the relationship between humans, health, and the environment. Students will begin the year by examining the ways humans impact the natural world, including biodiversity loss and pollution. The unit culminates with a study of the book Gather and an exploration of diverse perspectives on human relationships with the environment. Students will then investigate cells, disease, and the ways human activity has influenced the development, spread, and treatment of infectious and noninfectious diseases. The course concludes with an in-depth study of climate change, including its causes, impacts, and potential solutions, with a final emphasis on climate resilience and adaptation.
courses.notes: Integrated Science and ELA. Indicators addressed: Science 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, 6e, 4d, 1b, 2c, 5a, 3c

courses.description: This class is a challenging, fast-paced introduction to the study of chemistry and the central techniques and topics that chemists address. The course is structured in a spiraling manner, which means that topics will be interspersed with each other to favor understanding and long-term memory formation over memorization. We will connect the branches of chemistry into a multi-faceted yet cohesive whole. Instruction will include lecture, demonstrations, simulations, labs, and problem-solving. Students should expect to complete regular homework assignments, study for written assessments, and complete lab reports on their own.
courses.notes: Listed as 'Honors Chemistry-grade 11/12'. Indicators addressed will include: Science Years 3 & 4

courses.description: This elective will help you build a deeper understandings of rivers and the systems that shape them. We will learn about the physical, geologic, and ecosystems context of rivers through classroom instruction, hands-on activities, and field studies of local rivers. Students who sign up for this class should be prepared to go outside, to read and write, to work with maps, and to speak and listen. This course is open to students in grades 10-12 and is co-taught by Trevor Tait and Caleb Corliss.
courses.notes: Fall Semester elective. Co-taught by Trevor Tait and Caleb Corliss. Indicators addressed will include: Science Years 3 & 4

courses.description: This interdisciplinary course combines science and English language arts to help students build essential skills while exploring real-world topics in meaningful and engaging ways. Designed for students focused on graduation indicator recovery, this course blends reading, writing, scientific inquiry, and critical thinking. Students will explore themes and problems that connect across disciplines—such as environmental justice, human impact on ecosystems, or the science of storytelling—while also reinforcing key academic competencies. Math, social studies, and other subjects will be integrated where relevant to support a holistic understanding. This is a dynamic, project-based course—not a study hall—where students will actively participate in discussions, labs, research, and writing to meet learning goals and move confidently toward graduation.
courses.notes: Both semesters. Indicators addressed will include: Science 1d, 4a, 5c, 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, 6e

courses.description: Get ready to take science outside the classroom! In this hands-on field study course, students will explore the natural world through direct observation and investigation in outdoor environments. Blending topics from biology, ecology, environmental science, botany, and ornithology, students will gain a deeper understanding of local ecosystems, plant and animal life, and the dynamic relationships within nature. Classes will be held outdoors most days—rain or shine—so students should come prepared for the elements and ready to engage with the world around them. This course emphasizes scientific inquiry, data collection, and environmental awareness through real-world experiences.
courses.notes: 1 Semester--Fall. Indicators addressed: Science 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, 6e

courses.description: This is an honors science course. Students will be expected to be self directed, motivated learners. They will be expected to work independently, consistently meet deadlines, and show initiative. This course is content and terminology heavy, so keeping up with assignments is imperative to success in the course. Geology is best experienced in a hands-on lab and field environment, so expect frequent field trips. Courses can be taken individually but it is recommended that students take both semesters. This course is taught by Trevor Tait.

courses.description: How did we end up in the world we live in today? How can our study of history help us create joyful, resilient, connected futures? Modern World History students will define and explore the major trends and pivot points of the past 500 years, including European colonization and it’s modern day echoes Racial slavery and antiracist resistance movements The emergence of industrial society and the working class Revolutions and their effects on the world The rise of fascism and anti-fascist resistance The evolving political landscape of our world today
courses.notes: Freshmen full year. GC Indicators addressed: Inquiry (a-d)

courses.description: What happened since the end of World War II, and how does it effect the world students are preparing to help shape? How have every day people come together to fight for human rights, material improvements, and dignity, and how are they doing that today in our communities? Focal points may include the following, but are subject to input from students. Histories of intersectional feminism and indigenous feminist world views. The origins of environmental justice and migrant justice as frameworks for improving our communities. Why the U.S. healthcare system is the way it is, and the rise of neoliberal economic policy. Radical social movements of the 1960's and 70's, including the global decolonization movement, Black Panther Party, Young Lords, and more. Labor organizing and other contemporary social movements in and beyond Vermont.
courses.notes: GC Indicators addressed: Historical Thinking (a, c); Global Awareness (a, b)

courses.description: This class will focus on the “promises” of the Constitution and the founding of America as a nation. We will then explore the ways in which these promises have been unfulfilled throughout our history, in the past and the present. We will specifically cover the Civil War and the Reconstruction era, and the current consequences of that time period. We will then study the ways the people of this country have fought for a “more perfect union,” and sought to demand equal access to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. We’ll explore questions like: What structural inequities are embedded within our systems of governance? How have the people of this country responded to these inequities? How has the US constitution evolved over time to meet the needs of the time and its citizens? When have the promises of the Constitution been realized? Unrealized? Why?
courses.notes: Full Year (offered in Honors and Standard). Subtitle: The Building and Breaking of a Nation. Indicators addressed: Global Citizenship Inquiry 1A, 1B, 1C, 1D; Historical Thinking 2A, 2B, 2C; Civics, Government, and Society, 3A, 3B, 3C

courses.description: Explore how the concept of crime, and communities’ responses to crime, has evolved over time through a psychological, sociological and historical lens. We will also being preparing a trial to compete in the Vermont Mock Trial Competition. Explore questions like: How have we developed our moral understanding of right and wrong? What are the stories we tell about crime, “criminality,” and psychopathy? Who commits crime? What kind of crime? Why? How do other countries address crime? What other justice system models exist? End the course with a documentary film or podcast exploring a topic of your choice related to the criminal justice system. Final projects will be shared with our school and local community.
courses.notes: Spring Semester. Indicators addressed: Global Citizenship Inquiry 1A-1D; Historical Thinking 2A-2C; Civics, Government and Society 3A. Page also contains an older 'Criminal Justice - Spring' entry under 'not offered this year' (description beginning 'Taught by a former lawyer'); treated as the same course and not recorded separately.

courses.description: Let's roll up our sleeves and DO some democracy. The purpose of this class is to guide students through individual or group Civic Action Projects. CAPs are part of our new Twinfield Democracy Project and will help students earn the Civics Seal on their diplomas. Students will: Explore their identitites and values Learn about the systems of power and how to access them Research a topic of interest Develop a plan of action TAKE ACTION!
courses.notes: Indicators addressed: Global Citizenship Civics, Government and Society 3A

courses.description: What is the nature of reality? What is our moral duty to our fellow humans? What is beauty? These are just some of the questions we will tackle in our broad overview of philosophy We will learn the tools of logic and inquiry, which are useful in all walks of life.

of this class focuses on the development and practice of democracy in America. We will look at the historical foundations that shaped the Constitution, the compromises that were required to ratify the document, and the personalities that influenced that process. We will then look at how the Constitution has developed since its inception and how it impacts our daily lives. Semester two will examine the historic, economic, social and political events that helped shape the country that we live in today. This semester will be specifically targeting US history from the Civil War Era into the 21 st century. The American people and their experiences are the heart of this course. As we begin to understand the influences of the past, we will connect those influences to our present and our future. The main goal of this course is to develop responsible, critical thinking citizens!

The curriculum will cover a variety of topics. Possible topics include; psychology, depression, suicide prevention, nutrition, eating disorders, how to help a friend, refusal skills, addiction, reproductive systems, childbirth, methods of birth control, sexually transmitted infections, sexual harassment, healthy relationships, communication skills, CPR and more if there is time.

courses.description: Do you believe that all children deserve the resources and relationships necessary to achieve their dreams? Do you have a passion or idea that could make your community a better place? The DREAM Program is seeking curious, motivated and passionate students to engage in a hands-on course in youth mentoring and social change. In this experiential course of study, you will explore four primary themes—Mentorship, Identity, Sense of Place, and Meaning & Purpose—each of which seeks to answer a set of critical questions and prepare you to be an extraordinary mentor and contributing member of your community. Course work includes 4 classes a week, with one hands on day of being a supportive and fun mentor to a younger student. A time to explore and share interests, talents, passions, students will have an opportunity design an independent or group project that investigates what makes your community unique and special, as well as its areas for growth. Considering your place in your community, what change will you make? Projects can be designed based on student interest to gain proficiencies in art, Global Citizenship, or ELA.
courses.notes: program. Teachers: Pam Prim, Gabby Tatoyian, Pam Quinn. Projects can be designed to gain proficiencies in art, Global Citizenship, or ELA.
